analysis.one_liner: Makes war profiteering and fraud on military and reconstruction contracts a crime with 20-year prison terms.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime to defraud the United States or deliberately overvalue goods and services sold in connection with a war, military action, or relief and reconstruction work — the context was wartime contracting in Iraq. Violators could face up to 20 years in prison, a fine of at least $1 million or twice their profits, and loss of any property gained through the fraud. It also would let prosecutors pursue such cases anywhere in the world and treat the proceeds as subject to money-laundering laws.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers who fund military and reconstruction contracts, by adding a strong criminal deterrent to inflated invoices, false statements, and fraud by contractors and their executives.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a crime to run a scheme to defraud the United States or to materially overvalue a good or service with the specific intent to excessively profit from a war or reconstruction effort, punishable by up to 20 years in prison [S2] [S3].
Requires a fine of the greater of $1 million or twice the gross profits from the offense, and subjects the proceeds to civil and criminal forfeiture and to money-laundering laws [S2] [S3].
Gives federal prosecutors extraterritorial jurisdiction and flexible venue, so fraud committed overseas on U.S. contracts could still be prosecuted at home [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Government contractors and their executives who inflate prices or falsify records on wartime and reconstruction work; they would face prison, large fines, and seizure of profits.

drawbacks.text: Federal law already criminalizes fraud against the government and false claims, so the bill's main additions are harsher war-specific penalties and forfeiture — critics could argue existing statutes were sufficient and the new 'profiteering' standard adds vagueness [S2] [S3].

The bill applies broadly to any war, military action, or relief and reconstruction activity, with extraterritorial jurisdiction, language that honest contractors and subcontractors in complex wartime operations might worry sweeps too far [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aimed a heavy criminal penalty at a real and documented problem — overcharging and fraud in wartime contracting paid for by taxpayers — at little cost to honest contractors beyond stricter exposure. Its main weakness is overlap with existing fraud laws rather than any burden on ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it died quietly when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Leahy introduced the bill on March 2, 2006, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1] [S5].
The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action after the referral, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Contractors profiting from wartime and reconstruction work were better off: no new criminal penalties, profit-clawback fines, or forfeiture ever became law, and the record shows no one lifted a finger to move or oppose the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wartime contractors, whose profits went unchallenged

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the War Profiteering Prevention Act of 2006 and spoke for it at introduction, but had no cosponsors and no committee action followed.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to (chaired by Arlen Specter, R-PA, at the time)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; it died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows no votes and no opposition statements — the bill simply attracted no cosponsors of either party and never moved, so no partisan split appears in the record.

industries.industry: Defense and reconstruction contractors (Iraq-era wartime contracting)
industries.note: The bill would have exposed contractors and executives to 20-year prison terms, fines of at least $1 million or double their profits, and forfeiture for overvaluing goods or services or defrauding the government on war and reconstruction work. Its death left the existing penalties unchanged, so taxpayer-funded wartime contracts carried no added deterrent.
